items.title: Every measurement in a working lab traces back to seven international standards
items.claim: Every length, mass, temperature, current, time, light intensity and amount of substance measurement at any modern lab can be traced through calibration chains back to seven defined units maintained by international bodies. Calibration is what makes measurements comparable across labs.
items.prompt: What does 'traceable' mean for a measurement?

options.text: The instrument was calibrated against a reference standard, which itself was calibrated against a higher-tier standard, all the way back to the SI definition. Every step has a documented uncertainty
The instrument has a serial number
The measurement was published in a journal

items.reveal_title: Traceability chains and the redefined SI
items.reveal:
In 2019 the SI was redefined so all seven base units are now derived from fundamental constants: the speed of light defines the metre, the Planck constant defines the kilogram (since 2019, replacing the platinum-iridium reference cylinder), the Boltzmann constant defines the kelvin, and so on.

A national metrology institute (NPL in the UK, NIST in the US) maintains primary realisations of these units. Industry calibration labs are calibrated against these primaries. Working labs send instruments to industry labs for periodic calibration.

When you read a balance display in a school lab, the number you see has a chain of calibration certificates behind it linking it back to the Planck constant via a Kibble balance.
items.why: Calibration is treated as paperwork. It is the substrate that makes any quantitative claim comparable across labs, countries and decades.

items.title: Planes don't fly because of equal transit times
items.claim: Most textbooks say 'air travels faster over the top of a curved wing because it has further to go, so by Bernoulli the pressure is lower, so lift'. The premise is false — there is no rule that the air over the top and bottom must arrive at the same time.

options.text: Bernoulli effect, exactly as the textbook says

The wing deflects a mass of air downward (angle of attack and camber); by Newton's third law, the wing experiences an upward reaction force. Bernoulli is a valid but partial description — the air over the top really is faster, but for circulation/curvature reasons, not equal-transit
Engine thrust alone holds the plane up

items.reveal_title: Lift is downwash, and circulation explains the pressure difference
items.reveal:
High-speed flow visualisation shows air over the top of a wing arrives at the trailing edge BEFORE air below — equal-transit is wrong. Lift comes from the wing accelerating a column of air downward. By F equals ma, the wing must push air down; the air pushes the wing up.

The Bernoulli formula gives a self-consistent description of the pressure difference between top and bottom, but it doesn't explain WHY the air on top is faster. Modern aerodynamics uses circulation (the Kutta condition at the trailing edge) for that.

A flat plate at angle of attack generates lift just fine — no airfoil curvature required. Stunt planes fly upside down. Equal-transit is a story, not a mechanism.
items.why: Textbook physics often picks one principle and over-applies it. Real-world flight is best explained by momentum exchange, with Bernoulli as a consistency check.

items.title: A skydiver hits terminal velocity at around 55 m/s — and then doesn't get any faster
items.claim: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration. A skydiver in free fall accelerates from gravity (about 9.8 m/s²) — but only briefly. Air resistance grows with speed until it balances gravity exactly. Then acceleration stops and the speed plateaus.
items.prompt: Why does air resistance grow with speed?

options.text: Air gets denser at higher speeds

Drag force scales as v squared (at high Reynolds numbers): the faster you move, the more air molecules you displace per second, and each is hit harder. At some speed, drag exactly cancels weight and net force is zero
Friction with the parachute slows you down
The Earth attracts faster objects more weakly

items.reveal:
For a falling body in air: net force = mg - (1/2)ρ C_d A v² (gravity minus drag, where ρ is air density, C_d the drag coefficient, A the frontal area, v the speed).

At terminal velocity v_t, net force is zero: v_t = √(2mg / ρ C_d A). For a belly-down skydiver: m about 80 kg, A about 0.7 m², C_d about 1.0 — gives v_t about 55 m/s (200 km/h).

In a head-down dive (smaller A, lower C_d), the same skydiver can reach 120 m/s or more. Felix Baumgartner reached 1357 km/h in his stratospheric jump (2012) — air density was very low at altitude so terminal velocity was much higher.

Deploying a parachute increases A by a factor of ~50, reducing v_t to a manageable 5-7 m/s for landing.
items.why: Newton's law for falling is taught as 'gravity gives constant acceleration'. Air drag bends the rule and gives a steady-state speed — which is what makes skydiving and parachuting work.
